title: Berry v. Reagan — district preliminary injunction
citation: 32 Employment Practices Decisions (CCH) ¶ 31,304; No. 83-3182, 1983 WL 538 (D.D.C. November 14, 1983)
lead: Three commissioners challenge their removal, obtain preliminary protection, and then lose that judgment to mootness when the Commission’s authorized existence expires.

actors.name: Mary Frances Berry and other commissioners
actors.role: Challengers to President Reagan’s removal of three Civil Rights Commissioners.

actors.name: President Reagan
actors.role: President who removed the commissioners in 1983.

proceedings: The district court preliminarily blocked the removals.
On November 30, 1983, the D.C. Circuit vacated the judgment and directed dismissal as moot.
limits: The district opinion remains unrecovered. The assigned discussion supports the preliminary result; the later complete appellate order establishes vacatur, without deciding removal authority on the merits.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The President removes members of a commission situated in the executive branch
sections.cue: Why did the statutory label not end the disagreement?
paragraphs: In 1983 President Reagan removed three members of the Civil Rights Commission. Federal law then placed the Commission in the executive branch under 42 U.S.C. § 1975(a). Civil-rights groups and members of Congress nevertheless regarded its operations as independent and disputed the removals.

Mary Frances Berry and other commissioners challenged the President. The available account does not identify every plaintiff or reproduce individual appointment terms and removal letters. The dispute concerned whether executive-branch placement necessarily entailed unrestricted presidential removal authority.

sources.pinpoint: Assigned printed 190–191; distinct-stage account and controversy

sections.title: The district court temporarily protects the commissioners
sections.cue: How far did the reported ruling go?
paragraphs: The federal district court in the District of Columbia issued a preliminary injunction blocking the removals. Later judicial citations identify the decision as November 14, 1983. This was provisional protection, not a recovered final merits judgment setting out every tenure protection.

The complete district opinion is unavailable, so its full statutory analysis, constitutional reasoning and treatment of the preliminary-injunction factors cannot be reconstructed. The textbook’s discussion of the Commission’s investigative functions and its question whether Congress could appoint commissioners are editorial comparisons, not additional holdings attributed to this court.

sources.pinpoint: Assigned 190–191; supported district result and interpretive discussion

sections.title: Political restructuring is followed by appellate mootness
sections.cue: What became of the injunction without a merits decision?
paragraphs: The textbook reports a political compromise retaining two of the three commissioners and legislation expanding membership from six to eight while making the Commission independent. Those historical statements are distinct from findings in the missing district opinion.

The later appellate order states that the authorized existence of the Commission as then constituted had expired. On November 30, 1983, the D.C. Circuit vacated the district judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss the suit as moot. It neither affirmed nor rejected the district court’s removal analysis. The preliminary injunction therefore cannot be described as an appellate holding that Reagan lacked removal power.

sources.pinpoint: Assigned 190 and later order, 732 F.2d 949; subsequent disposition
